questions.question: Which data structure follows the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle?
questions.correctAnswer: Stack
questions.explanation: A stack removes the most recently added element first — this is the LIFO property.

questions.question: In a singly linked list each node contains data and what else?
options: A pointer to the previous node
A pointer to the next node
The total size of the list
questions.correctAnswer: A pointer to the next node
questions.explanation: Each node in a singly linked list stores data and a reference (pointer) to the next node in the sequence.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of children a node can have in a binary tree?
questions.explanation: By definition a binary tree node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.

questions.question: Which data structure uses First In First Out (FIFO) ordering?
questions.correctAnswer: Queue
questions.explanation: A queue processes elements in the order they were added — the first element enqueued is the first dequeued.

questions.question: What does a hash table use to map keys to array indices?
questions.correctAnswer: Hash function
questions.explanation: A hash function computes an index from the key so the value can be stored and retrieved in near-constant time.

questions.question: Which traversal visits the root node before its subtrees?
questions.correctAnswer: Pre-order
questions.explanation: Pre-order traversal visits the root first then recursively visits the left subtree followed by the right subtree.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
questions.explanation: Arrays support constant-time random access because elements are stored in contiguous memory locations.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting into a hash table with chaining?
questions.correctAnswer: O(n)
questions.explanation: If all keys hash to the same bucket the chain becomes a linked list of length n so insertion degrades to O(n).

questions.question: Which self-balancing BST guarantees O(log n) height by enforcing a color invariant on every node?
questions.correctAnswer: Red-Black Tree
questions.explanation: A Red-Black Tree colors every node red or black and enforces rules that keep the longest path at most twice the shortest guaranteeing O(log n) height.

questions.question: In a min-heap which element is always at the root?
questions.correctAnswer: The smallest element
questions.explanation: A min-heap maintains the heap property: every parent is less than or equal to its children so the minimum is always at the root.

questions.question: What is the amortized time complexity of appending to a dynamic array that doubles in size when full?
questions.explanation: Although individual resizes cost O(n) they happen rarely enough that the amortized cost per append is O(1).

questions.question: Which data structure is best suited for implementing an LRU cache?
questions.correctAnswer: HashMap + Doubly Linked List
questions.explanation: An LRU cache needs O(1) lookup (hash map) and O(1) insertion/removal of the least-recently-used item (doubly linked list).

questions.question: What is the space complexity of storing a graph with V vertices and E edges using an adjacency list?
questions.correctAnswer: O(V + E)
questions.explanation: An adjacency list stores a list of neighbors for each vertex using O(V) vertex entries plus O(E) edge entries total.

questions.question: After deleting the root of a max-heap how is the heap property restored?
options: Swap root with last element then heapify down
questions.correctAnswer: Swap root with last element then heapify down
questions.explanation: The last element replaces the root then sift-down (heapify) swaps it with its larger child repeatedly until the max-heap property holds.

questions.question: A Bloom filter may return false positives but never false negatives. Why is this the case?
options: It uses multiple hash functions mapping to a bit array
It uses a sorted array with binary search
It discards elements after a timeout
questions.correctAnswer: It uses multiple hash functions mapping to a bit array
questions.explanation: A Bloom filter sets bits at multiple hash positions. A lookup checks all positions — an absent element may collide with bits set by other elements (false positive) but a present element always has all its bits set (no false negative).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array using the bottom-up method?
questions.correctAnswer: O(n)
questions.explanation: Bottom-up heap construction calls heapify on each non-leaf node. The total work sums to O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom and require few swaps.

questions.question: In a B-tree of minimum degree t what is the maximum number of keys a node can hold?
questions.explanation: A B-tree node of minimum degree t can hold at most 2t − 1 keys and 2t children. This keeps the tree balanced and optimizes disk reads.

questions.question: Which data structure supports union and find operations in nearly O(1) amortized time using path compression and union by rank?
questions.correctAnswer: Disjoint Set (Union-Find)
questions.explanation: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank achieves an amortized time complexity of O(α(n)) per operation where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant.

questions.question: What problem does a skip list solve compared to a standard sorted linked list?
questions.correctAnswer: O(log n) expected search time
questions.explanation: A skip list adds multiple levels of forward pointers to a sorted linked list enabling binary-search-like behavior with O(log n) expected time for search insert and delete.

questions.question: In a segment tree built over an array of n elements how many nodes does the tree contain in the worst case?
questions.correctAnswer: 4n
questions.explanation: A segment tree is typically allocated as a complete binary tree. For n elements the array representation may need up to 4n nodes to handle non-power-of-two sizes safely.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of a Fibonacci heap over a binary heap for Dijkstra's algorithm?
questions.correctAnswer: O(1) amortized decrease-key
questions.explanation: Fibonacci heaps support decrease-key in O(1) amortized time reducing Dijkstra's total complexity to O(V log V + E) compared to O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap.

questions.question: What does Big-O notation describe about an algorithm?
options: The exact running time in seconds
An upper bound on growth rate as input size increases
questions.correctAnswer: An upper bound on growth rate as input size increases
questions.explanation: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound on how an algorithm's time or space requirements grow relative to input size.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly finds the minimum element and places it at the beginning?
questions.correctAnswer: Selection Sort
questions.explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted portion for the minimum element and swaps it into the next sorted position on each pass.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of linear search in the worst case?
questions.correctAnswer: O(n)
questions.explanation: Linear search checks each element one by one — in the worst case the target is last or absent requiring n comparisons.

questions.question: Binary search requires the input array to be in what state?
questions.correctAnswer: Sorted
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space at each step which only works correctly when the array is sorted.

questions.question: Which algorithm technique solves a problem by breaking it into smaller subproblems solving each recursively and combining results?
questions.correctAnswer: Divide and Conquer
questions.explanation: Divide and conquer splits the problem into independent subproblems solves them recursively and merges the solutions.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort in the worst case?
questions.correctAnswer: O(n²)
questions.explanation: Bubble sort makes n passes through the array swapping adjacent elements — nested loops give O(n²) in the worst case.

questions.question: Which search algorithm works by checking every element one by one from start to end?
questions.correctAnswer: Linear Search
questions.explanation: Linear search iterates through the collection sequentially comparing each element with the target.

questions.question: What is the average-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
questions.correctAnswer: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Quick sort's average case partitions the array into roughly equal halves at each level of recursion giving O(n log n) comparisons.

questions.question: Which algorithmic paradigm stores solutions to overlapping subproblems to avoid redundant computation?
questions.correctAnswer: Dynamic Programming
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming identifies overlapping subproblems and stores their results (memoization or tabulation) so each subproblem is solved only once.

questions.question: In Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm why must all edge weights be non-negative?
options: The greedy choice assumes shorter partial paths remain shorter
The algorithm only works on trees
questions.correctAnswer: The greedy choice assumes shorter partial paths remain shorter
questions.explanation: Dijkstra greedily finalizes the shortest known distance to a node. A negative edge could later provide a shorter path to an already-finalized node violating this greedy invariant.

questions.question: What is the recurrence relation for Merge Sort?
questions.explanation: Merge sort splits the array into two halves (2 subproblems of size n/2) and merges them in O(n) time.

questions.question: Which graph traversal algorithm uses a queue and visits nodes level by level?
questions.correctAnswer: Breadth-First Search
questions.explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue to explore all neighbors at the current depth before moving to the next level.

questions.question: A greedy algorithm for the activity selection problem sorts activities by what criterion?
questions.correctAnswer: Finish time
questions.explanation: Sorting by finish time and always picking the next compatible activity yields the maximum number of non-overlapping activities — a classic greedy strategy.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort and when does it occur?
options: O(n log n) when the array is sorted
O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
O(n) when all elements are equal
O(n²) when the array is random
questions.correctAnswer: O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
questions.explanation: If the pivot consistently produces maximally unbalanced partitions (e.g. already sorted array with first-element pivot) recursion depth reaches n and total work becomes O(n²).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matching algorithm?
questions.correctAnswer: O(n + m)
questions.explanation: KMP preprocesses the pattern to build a failure function in O(m) then scans the text in O(n) — total O(n + m) without backtracking on the text.

questions.question: Which problem is solved by finding a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum total weight in a complete graph?
questions.correctAnswer: Travelling Salesman Problem
questions.explanation: The TSP asks for the minimum-cost tour visiting every vertex exactly once and returning to the start — a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum weight.

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem directly solve?
options: Recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
questions.correctAnswer: Recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
questions.explanation: The Master Theorem applies to divide-and-conquer recurrences where the problem splits into a subproblems each of size n/b with combine cost f(n).

questions.question: In the context of NP-completeness what does a polynomial-time reduction from problem A to problem B prove?
options: B is at least as hard as A
A and B have the same solution
B can be solved in polynomial time
questions.correctAnswer: B is at least as hard as A
questions.explanation: If A ≤ₚ B then any polynomial-time algorithm for B would also solve A — so B is at least as hard as A.

questions.question: Which algorithm finds the strongly connected components of a directed graph in O(V + E) time?
questions.correctAnswer: Tarjan's algorithm
questions.explanation: Tarjan's SCC algorithm uses a single DFS pass with a stack and low-link values to identify all strongly connected components in linear time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path algorithm?
questions.correctAnswer: O(V³)
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall uses three nested loops over V vertices to consider every intermediate vertex for every pair giving O(V³).

questions.question: In a maximum-flow network what does the max-flow min-cut theorem state?
options: Maximum flow equals minimum edge weight
Maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut
Maximum flow equals the number of paths
Flow is always equal to demand
questions.correctAnswer: Maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut
questions.explanation: The theorem proves that the value of the maximum flow from source to sink equals the total capacity of the edges in the minimum s-t cut.

questions.question: What does SQL stand for?
questions.correctAnswer: Structured Query Language
questions.explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing and querying relational databases.

questions.question: Which SQL keyword is used to retrieve data from a database?
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT
questions.explanation: The SELECT statement queries one or more tables and returns the matching rows as a result set.

questions.question: A primary key in a relational database must be what?
questions.correctAnswer: Unique and not null
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table and by definition cannot contain NULL values.

questions.question: Which type of database relationship links one record in table A to many records in table B?
questions.correctAnswer: One-to-Many
questions.explanation: A one-to-many relationship means a single row in table A can relate to multiple rows in table B — for example one department having many employees.

questions.question: What does the WHERE clause do in a SQL query?
options: Filters rows based on a condition
questions.correctAnswer: Filters rows based on a condition
questions.explanation: The WHERE clause specifies a condition that each row must satisfy to be included in the query results.

questions.question: Which SQL command is used to add a new row to a table?
questions.correctAnswer: INSERT
questions.explanation: INSERT INTO adds a new row of data to an existing table.

questions.question: What is a foreign key?
options: A column that references the primary key of another table
A unique identifier within the same table
questions.correctAnswer: A column that references the primary key of another table
questions.explanation: A foreign key creates a link between two tables by referencing the primary key in the parent table enforcing referential integrity.

questions.question: What is the purpose of database normalization?
options: To reduce data redundancy and improve integrity
questions.correctAnswer: To reduce data redundancy and improve integrity
questions.explanation: Normalization organizes tables to minimize duplicate data and dependency anomalies — each fact is stored in exactly one place.

questions.question: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependencies?
questions.correctAnswer: Third Normal Form (3NF)
questions.explanation: 3NF requires that every non-key attribute depends only on the primary key — not transitively through another non-key attribute.

questions.question: What is the ACID property 'Atomicity' in database transactions?
options: All transactions run at the same time
Transactions are isolated from each other
questions.correctAnswer: A transaction is all-or-nothing
questions.explanation: Atomicity guarantees that either all operations in a transaction complete successfully or none of them take effect — partial execution is impossible.

questions.question: Which type of SQL JOIN returns only the rows with matching values in both tables?
questions.correctAnswer: INNER JOIN
questions.explanation: An INNER JOIN returns only those rows where the join condition is satisfied in both tables — unmatched rows are excluded.

questions.question: What does a database index primarily improve?
questions.correctAnswer: Read query performance
questions.explanation: An index creates a sorted data structure (like a B-tree) that lets the database locate rows much faster than scanning the entire table.

questions.question: In a relational database what is a view?
options: A physical copy of a table
A virtual table defined by a stored query
questions.correctAnswer: A virtual table defined by a stored query
questions.explanation: A view is a named SELECT query that behaves like a table but does not store data itself — it dynamically retrieves data when queried.

questions.question: What is a deadlock in database systems?
options: A query that takes too long
Two transactions waiting for each other's locks indefinitely
questions.correctAnswer: Two transactions waiting for each other's locks indefinitely
questions.explanation: A deadlock occurs when transaction A holds lock X and waits for lock Y while transaction B holds Y and waits for X — neither can proceed.

questions.question: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
options: Clustered indexes are faster; non-clustered are slower
A clustered index determines physical row order; a non-clustered index uses a separate structure pointing to rows
Clustered indexes work on views; non-clustered indexes work on tables
questions.correctAnswer: A clustered index determines physical row order; a non-clustered index uses a separate structure pointing to rows
questions.explanation: A clustered index sorts and stores table rows by the index key (one per table). A non-clustered index maintains a separate B-tree with pointers back to the data rows.

questions.question: In the context of ACID what does the Isolation level 'Serializable' guarantee?
options: Transactions execute as if they were run one after another
questions.correctAnswer: Transactions execute as if they were run one after another
questions.explanation: Serializable is the strictest isolation level — it ensures concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial execution order preventing all anomalies.

questions.question: What problem can occur at the 'Read Committed' isolation level but not at 'Repeatable Read'?
questions.correctAnswer: Non-repeatable reads
questions.explanation: At Read Committed a transaction may see different values for the same row if another transaction commits between reads. Repeatable Read prevents this by locking read rows.

questions.question: What is a write-ahead log (WAL) and why is it important?
options: A log written after transaction commit for auditing
A log written before changes are applied to disk ensuring crash recovery
questions.correctAnswer: A log written before changes are applied to disk ensuring crash recovery
questions.explanation: WAL writes all modifications to a log file before applying them to data pages. After a crash the log can replay committed changes and undo uncommitted ones.

questions.question: Which concurrency control protocol uses timestamps to order transactions without locks?
questions.correctAnswer: Timestamp Ordering Protocol
questions.explanation: The timestamp ordering protocol assigns a unique timestamp to each transaction and ensures read/write operations follow timestamp order — aborting transactions that violate the order.

questions.question: In query optimization what does a cost-based optimizer use to choose an execution plan?
options: The length of the SQL statement
Statistics about table sizes and index selectivity
The order of columns in the SELECT clause
questions.correctAnswer: Statistics about table sizes and index selectivity
questions.explanation: A cost-based optimizer estimates the I/O and CPU cost of different plans using statistics like row counts histogram distributions and index cardinality to pick the cheapest plan.

questions.question: What is the CAP theorem in distributed databases?
options: Consistency Availability and Performance can all be achieved
You can guarantee at most two of Consistency Availability and Partition tolerance simultaneously
CAP only applies to NoSQL databases
questions.correctAnswer: You can guarantee at most two of Consistency Availability and Partition tolerance simultaneously
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot guarantee all three.

questions.question: What is the primary function of an operating system?
options: Manage hardware resources and provide services to applications
questions.correctAnswer: Manage hardware resources and provide services to applications
questions.explanation: An OS acts as an intermediary between applications and hardware — managing CPU memory storage and I/O devices.

questions.question: What is a process in an operating system?
options: A program in execution with its own memory and state
questions.correctAnswer: A program in execution with its own memory and state
questions.explanation: A process is a running instance of a program including its code data stack program counter and allocated resources.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm gives each process an equal time slice in round-robin fashion?
questions.correctAnswer: Round Robin
questions.explanation: Round Robin assigns a fixed time quantum to each process cycling through the ready queue — ensuring fair CPU sharing.

questions.question: What is virtual memory?
options: Memory on an external USB drive
A technique that uses disk space to extend available RAM
questions.correctAnswer: A technique that uses disk space to extend available RAM
questions.explanation: Virtual memory maps address spaces to physical RAM and disk so programs can use more memory than physically available. The OS swaps pages between RAM and disk as needed.

questions.question: What is the difference between a thread and a process?
options: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process sharing its memory space
questions.correctAnswer: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process sharing its memory space
questions.explanation: Threads within the same process share code data and resources but each has its own stack and program counter. Processes have separate memory spaces.

questions.question: What does the kernel of an operating system do?
options: Provides the core services including process scheduling and memory management
questions.correctAnswer: Provides the core services including process scheduling and memory management
questions.explanation: The kernel is the core component of the OS — it manages CPU scheduling memory allocation device I/O and system calls.

questions.question: What is a system call?
options: A phone call to tech support
An interface for user programs to request services from the OS kernel
questions.correctAnswer: An interface for user programs to request services from the OS kernel
questions.explanation: System calls provide a controlled gateway for user-space programs to request kernel services like file I/O process creation and memory allocation.

questions.question: What is a race condition?
options: When two programs compete for CPU time
When the outcome depends on the unpredictable order of thread execution
When a process runs too fast
questions.correctAnswer: When the outcome depends on the unpredictable order of thread execution
questions.explanation: A race condition occurs when multiple threads access shared data concurrently and the result depends on the timing of their execution — leading to unpredictable behavior.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a mutex (mutual exclusion lock)?
options: To ensure only one thread accesses a critical section at a time
questions.correctAnswer: To ensure only one thread accesses a critical section at a time
questions.explanation: A mutex prevents concurrent access to a shared resource — a thread must acquire the lock before entering the critical section and release it when done.

questions.question: Which page replacement algorithm is optimal but impractical to implement?
questions.correctAnswer: Optimal (Bélády's)
questions.explanation: The optimal algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. It requires future knowledge making it impractical but useful as a benchmark.

questions.question: What is thrashing in the context of virtual memory?
options: Excessive page faults causing the system to spend more time swapping than executing
questions.correctAnswer: Excessive page faults causing the system to spend more time swapping than executing
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the working set of active pages exceeds available physical memory — the OS constantly swaps pages in and out and useful work drops dramatically.

questions.question: What are the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?
options: Mutual exclusion — hold and wait — no preemption — circular wait
Starvation — livelock — priority inversion — race condition
Mutual exclusion — FIFO — aging — round robin
questions.correctAnswer: Mutual exclusion — hold and wait — no preemption — circular wait
questions.explanation: Coffman's conditions state that deadlock requires all four: mutual exclusion hold-and-wait no preemption and circular wait. Preventing any one condition prevents deadlock.

questions.question: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
options: In preemptive scheduling the OS can forcibly suspend a running process; in non-preemptive it cannot
Preemptive scheduling is only for I/O-bound processes
questions.correctAnswer: In preemptive scheduling the OS can forcibly suspend a running process; in non-preemptive it cannot
questions.explanation: Preemptive schedulers can interrupt a running process (e.g. when its time quantum expires) while non-preemptive schedulers let each process run until it voluntarily yields or completes.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
options: To cache virtual-to-physical address translations for faster memory access
questions.correctAnswer: To cache virtual-to-physical address translations for faster memory access
questions.explanation: The TLB is a hardware cache that stores recent page table entries. On a TLB hit the CPU skips the page table walk — dramatically speeding up memory access.

questions.question: Explain the Banker's algorithm. What type of deadlock strategy does it implement?
questions.correctAnswer: Deadlock avoidance
questions.explanation: The Banker's algorithm is a deadlock avoidance strategy. Before granting a resource request it checks whether the system would remain in a safe state — if not the request is deferred.

questions.question: What is priority inversion and how does priority inheritance solve it?
options: A high-priority process runs first; inheritance gives it more CPU
A low-priority task holding a lock blocks a high-priority task; priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority
Priority is inverted when the scheduler fails; inheritance resets it
It only occurs in real-time systems and has no solution
questions.correctAnswer: A low-priority task holding a lock blocks a high-priority task; priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority
questions.explanation: Priority inversion occurs when a medium-priority task preempts a low-priority one that holds a lock needed by a high-priority task. Priority inheritance boosts the lock holder to prevent this.

questions.question: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?
options: Internal wastes space inside allocated blocks; external wastes space between allocated blocks
Internal is on disk; external is in RAM
Internal is caused by paging; external is caused by segmentation only
questions.correctAnswer: Internal wastes space inside allocated blocks; external wastes space between allocated blocks
questions.explanation: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated memory exceeds what the process needs (e.g. fixed-size pages). External fragmentation occurs when free memory is scattered in small non-contiguous chunks.

questions.question: How does Copy-on-Write (COW) optimize the fork() system call?
options: It copies the entire process memory immediately
It shares pages between parent and child and copies only when either writes to a page
It avoids creating a child process
It compresses the memory before copying
questions.correctAnswer: It shares pages between parent and child and copies only when either writes to a page
questions.explanation: COW marks shared pages as read-only after fork(). A write triggers a page fault which copies just that page — avoiding the cost of duplicating the entire address space upfront.

questions.question: What is the difference between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel?
options: A monolithic kernel runs all OS services in kernel space; a microkernel runs minimal services in kernel space and the rest in user space
Microkernels are faster because they have fewer features
questions.correctAnswer: A monolithic kernel runs all OS services in kernel space; a microkernel runs minimal services in kernel space and the rest in user space
questions.explanation: Monolithic kernels (e.g. Linux) include drivers file systems and networking in kernel mode. Microkernels (e.g. Minix) keep only IPC scheduling and memory management in the kernel — other services run as user processes.

questions.question: What is Bélády's anomaly in page replacement?
options: Adding more pages always reduces page faults
With FIFO replacement increasing the number of page frames can sometimes increase page faults
It means pages are loaded in the wrong order
questions.correctAnswer: With FIFO replacement increasing the number of page frames can sometimes increase page faults
questions.explanation: Bélády's anomaly is counterintuitive: for FIFO page replacement certain reference strings cause more page faults with more frames. Stack-based algorithms like LRU never exhibit this anomaly.

questions.question: In a real-time operating system what is the difference between hard and soft real-time constraints?
options: Hard real-time requires deadlines to be met absolutely; soft real-time allows occasional deadline misses
Soft real-time is only for multimedia
questions.correctAnswer: Hard real-time requires deadlines to be met absolutely; soft real-time allows occasional deadline misses
questions.explanation: In hard real-time systems (e.g. aircraft control) missing a deadline is a system failure. Soft real-time (e.g. video streaming) tolerates occasional misses with degraded quality.

questions.question: What does IP stand for in networking?
questions.correctAnswer: Internet Protocol
questions.explanation: The Internet Protocol (IP) is responsible for addressing and routing packets across networks to their destination.

questions.question: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for end-to-end data transfer and error recovery?
questions.correctAnswer: Transport
questions.explanation: The Transport layer (Layer 4) provides reliable end-to-end communication through segmentation flow control and error recovery — e.g. TCP.

questions.question: What is the purpose of DNS in networking?
options: To translate domain names into IP addresses
questions.correctAnswer: To translate domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: The Domain Name System maps human-readable domain names (like google.com) to IP addresses so browsers can locate servers.

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
options: TCP provides reliable ordered delivery while UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable
UDP is used only for email
TCP does not use IP addresses
questions.correctAnswer: TCP provides reliable ordered delivery while UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable
questions.explanation: TCP ensures packets arrive in order with error checking and retransmission. UDP sends packets without guarantees — useful for real-time applications like video calls.

questions.question: What does a router do in a computer network?
options: Forwards data packets between different networks based on IP addresses
questions.correctAnswer: Forwards data packets between different networks based on IP addresses
questions.explanation: A router examines the destination IP of each packet and forwards it toward its destination using routing tables.

questions.question: What is a MAC address?
options: A unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card
The same as an IP address
questions.correctAnswer: A unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card
questions.explanation: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a 48-bit hardware address burned into a NIC — used for communication within a local network segment.

questions.question: What is a subnet mask used for?
options: To determine which portion of an IP address identifies the network vs. the host
questions.correctAnswer: To determine which portion of an IP address identifies the network vs. the host
questions.explanation: A subnet mask separates the network prefix from the host portion of an IP address allowing routers to determine if a destination is local or remote.

questions.question: What is the three-way handshake in TCP?
options: The SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK sequence used to establish a TCP connection
A way to terminate a connection
questions.correctAnswer: The SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK sequence used to establish a TCP connection
questions.explanation: The client sends SYN the server replies with SYN-ACK and the client confirms with ACK. This establishes a reliable connection before data transfer begins.

questions.question: What is the purpose of ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)?
options: To resolve an IP address to a MAC address on a local network
To route packets across the internet
questions.correctAnswer: To resolve an IP address to a MAC address on a local network
questions.explanation: When a host knows the destination IP but needs the MAC address for the local link it broadcasts an ARP request. The target replies with its MAC address.

questions.question: What is NAT (Network Address Translation) used for?
options: To allow multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address
questions.correctAnswer: To allow multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address
questions.explanation: NAT translates private IP addresses to a public IP for outgoing traffic and maps responses back — enabling many devices to access the internet through one public address.

questions.question: What is the difference between a hub and a switch?
options: A hub broadcasts to all ports while a switch forwards frames only to the destination port
A switch is wireless and a hub is wired
questions.correctAnswer: A hub broadcasts to all ports while a switch forwards frames only to the destination port
questions.explanation: A hub is a simple repeater that sends incoming frames to every port. A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the correct port — reducing collisions.

questions.question: What is CIDR notation and why is it used?
options: A compact representation of IP address ranges (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) that enables flexible subnetting
questions.correctAnswer: A compact representation of IP address ranges (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) that enables flexible subnetting
questions.explanation: CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaces the rigid Class A/B/C system allowing networks to be subdivided into subnets of any size by specifying the prefix length.

questions.question: How does DHCP assign IP addresses to devices on a network?
options: By reading the device's MAC address only
questions.correctAnswer: Through a Discover-Offer-Request-Acknowledge (DORA) process
questions.explanation: A DHCP client broadcasts a Discover message. The server responds with an Offer. The client sends a Request and the server confirms with an Acknowledge — dynamically assigning an IP.

questions.question: What does a firewall do?
options: Monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules
questions.correctAnswer: Monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules
questions.explanation: A firewall inspects packets against a set of rules and decides whether to allow or block traffic — protecting networks from unauthorized access and attacks.

questions.question: How does TCP handle congestion control?
options: Through algorithms like Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance that dynamically adjust the sending rate
questions.correctAnswer: Through algorithms like Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance that dynamically adjust the sending rate
questions.explanation: TCP starts with a small congestion window (slow start) doubling it each RTT until loss occurs. Then it switches to congestion avoidance (additive increase) and halves the window on loss (multiplicative decrease).

questions.question: What is the difference between distance-vector and link-state routing protocols?
options: Distance-vector routers share routing tables with neighbors; link-state routers flood topology information to all routers
questions.correctAnswer: Distance-vector routers share routing tables with neighbors; link-state routers flood topology information to all routers
questions.explanation: Distance-vector protocols (e.g. RIP) exchange distance tables with direct neighbors. Link-state protocols (e.g. OSPF) flood link-state advertisements so every router builds a complete topology map and runs Dijkstra.

questions.question: What is BGP and why is it called the 'protocol of the internet'?
options: The Border Gateway Protocol — it manages routing between autonomous systems that make up the internet
questions.correctAnswer: The Border Gateway Protocol — it manages routing between autonomous systems that make up the internet
questions.explanation: BGP is the exterior gateway protocol that enables autonomous systems (ISPs and large networks) to exchange reachability information — forming the global internet routing table.

questions.question: How does TLS (Transport Layer Security) establish a secure connection?
options: Through a handshake that negotiates cipher suites exchanges certificates and derives session keys
By using UDP instead of TCP
questions.correctAnswer: Through a handshake that negotiates cipher suites exchanges certificates and derives session keys
questions.explanation: The TLS handshake includes: client hello → server hello + certificate → key exchange → session key derivation. This establishes an encrypted channel before application data flows.

questions.question: What is the count-to-infinity problem in distance-vector routing?
options: After a link failure routers slowly increment distance metrics through update loops before converging
questions.correctAnswer: After a link failure routers slowly increment distance metrics through update loops before converging
questions.explanation: When a link fails distance-vector protocols can enter a loop where routers keep incrementing the cost metric — converging very slowly. Solutions include split horizon and poison reverse.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the sliding window protocol in TCP?
options: To allow the sender to transmit multiple segments before requiring an acknowledgment improving throughput
questions.correctAnswer: To allow the sender to transmit multiple segments before requiring an acknowledgment improving throughput
questions.explanation: The sliding window allows multiple unacknowledged segments to be in flight. The window size adjusts based on receiver capacity (flow control) and network conditions (congestion control).

questions.question: How does an ARP spoofing attack work and what is its impact?
options: It floods the network with DNS requests
An attacker sends fake ARP replies to associate their MAC with a victim's IP enabling man-in-the-middle attacks
questions.correctAnswer: An attacker sends fake ARP replies to associate their MAC with a victim's IP enabling man-in-the-middle attacks
questions.explanation: ARP has no authentication. An attacker can send unsolicited ARP replies mapping a legitimate IP to their own MAC — intercepting traffic intended for that IP.

questions.question: What is encapsulation in object-oriented programming?
options: Bundling data and methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access
questions.correctAnswer: Bundling data and methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state behind methods — external code interacts through a public interface without knowing the implementation details.

questions.question: What is inheritance in OOP?
options: A mechanism where a new class derives properties and behavior from an existing class
questions.correctAnswer: A mechanism where a new class derives properties and behavior from an existing class
questions.explanation: Inheritance allows a child class to reuse and extend the functionality of a parent class — promoting code reuse and hierarchical design.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
options: The ability of different classes to be treated through the same interface while behaving differently
questions.correctAnswer: The ability of different classes to be treated through the same interface while behaving differently
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets a method call behave differently depending on the object's actual type — e.g. calling draw() on a Circle vs. a Rectangle produces different results.

questions.question: What is a class in OOP?
options: A blueprint for creating objects that defines attributes and methods
questions.correctAnswer: A blueprint for creating objects that defines attributes and methods
questions.explanation: A class defines the structure (attributes) and behavior (methods) that its instances (objects) will have.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
options: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of that class
questions.correctAnswer: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of that class
questions.explanation: A class defines the template. An object is a concrete instance created from that class with its own attribute values stored in memory.

questions.question: What is a constructor?
options: A special method called automatically when an object is created to initialize its state
questions.correctAnswer: A special method called automatically when an object is created to initialize its state
questions.explanation: A constructor initializes the object's attributes when it is instantiated — e.g. __init__ in Python or the class-named method in Java/C++.

questions.question: What does the 'this' (or 'self') keyword refer to in a method?
options: The current instance of the class on which the method is called
questions.correctAnswer: The current instance of the class on which the method is called
questions.explanation: 'this' (Java/C++) or 'self' (Python) refers to the specific object invoking the method — allowing access to its own attributes and other methods.

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
options: Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class; overriding redefines a parent method in a child class
Overriding requires a new class name
questions.correctAnswer: Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class; overriding redefines a parent method in a child class
questions.explanation: Overloading is compile-time polymorphism (same method name different signatures). Overriding is runtime polymorphism (child replaces parent's method with its own implementation).

questions.question: What is an abstract class?
options: A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement
A class that is automatically deleted
questions.correctAnswer: A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement
questions.explanation: Abstract classes define a contract — they can have both implemented and abstract (unimplemented) methods. Subclasses must provide implementations for the abstract methods.

questions.question: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
options: An interface declares method signatures without implementation (prior to Java 8); an abstract class can include both implemented and abstract methods
questions.correctAnswer: An interface declares method signatures without implementation (prior to Java 8); an abstract class can include both implemented and abstract methods
questions.explanation: Interfaces define a pure contract. Abstract classes can share common code. A class can implement multiple interfaces but typically extends only one abstract class.

questions.question: What is the SOLID principle 'Single Responsibility'?
options: A class should have only one method
A class should have only one reason to change
A variable should hold only one value
A function should have only one parameter
questions.correctAnswer: A class should have only one reason to change
questions.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle states each class should be responsible for one aspect of functionality — reducing coupling and making changes localized.

questions.question: What is composition in OOP and how does it differ from inheritance?
options: Composition is the same as inheritance
Composition builds complex objects by containing instances of other classes rather than inheriting from them
questions.correctAnswer: Composition builds complex objects by containing instances of other classes rather than inheriting from them
questions.explanation: Composition uses a 'has-a' relationship (a Car has an Engine) while inheritance uses an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog is an Animal). Composition is generally more flexible.

questions.question: What is the purpose of access modifiers like public private and protected?
options: To control the visibility and accessibility of class members
questions.correctAnswer: To control the visibility and accessibility of class members
questions.explanation: Access modifiers enforce encapsulation: private restricts access to the class itself protected adds access for subclasses and public allows access from anywhere.

questions.question: What is a design pattern in OOP?
options: A reusable solution template for a commonly occurring software design problem
questions.correctAnswer: A reusable solution template for a commonly occurring software design problem
questions.explanation: Design patterns (like Singleton Factory Observer) provide proven approaches to recurring design challenges — they are not code but templates for how to structure solutions.

questions.question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle and why does violating it cause bugs?
options: Subclasses should always override all parent methods
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without altering program correctness
It requires all classes to be abstract
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without altering program correctness
questions.explanation: LSP means subclasses must honor the contract of their parent. Violating it (e.g. a Square subclass of Rectangle that breaks setWidth/setHeight expectations) causes subtle bugs when code uses the parent type.

questions.question: What problem does the Dependency Inversion Principle solve?
options: High-level modules depending on low-level implementation details making the system rigid
questions.correctAnswer: High-level modules depending on low-level implementation details making the system rigid
questions.explanation: DIP states that high-level modules should depend on abstractions not concretions. This allows swapping implementations (e.g. switching databases) without modifying business logic.

questions.question: How does the Observer pattern work and when should it be used?
options: Subjects maintain a list of observers and notify them of state changes — useful for event-driven architectures
questions.correctAnswer: Subjects maintain a list of observers and notify them of state changes — useful for event-driven architectures
questions.explanation: The Observer pattern decouples event producers from consumers. When the subject's state changes all registered observers are automatically notified — used in GUIs event systems and reactive programming.

questions.question: What is the diamond problem in multiple inheritance and how do languages solve it?
options: Ambiguity when a class inherits from two classes that share a common ancestor — solved by virtual inheritance or interfaces
questions.correctAnswer: Ambiguity when a class inherits from two classes that share a common ancestor — solved by virtual inheritance or interfaces
questions.explanation: If class D inherits from B and C which both inherit from A then D has two copies of A's members. C++ uses virtual inheritance; Java/C# avoid the problem by allowing only single class inheritance with multiple interfaces.

questions.question: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy of an object?
options: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares references to nested objects; a deep copy recursively duplicates all nested objects
questions.correctAnswer: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares references to nested objects; a deep copy recursively duplicates all nested objects
questions.explanation: With a shallow copy modifying a nested object in the copy also affects the original. Deep copy creates fully independent copies at all levels — important for mutable nested structures.

questions.question: How does the Strategy pattern differ from the Template Method pattern?
options: Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms at runtime; Template Method uses inheritance to let subclasses override specific steps
questions.correctAnswer: Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms at runtime; Template Method uses inheritance to let subclasses override specific steps
questions.explanation: Strategy encapsulates algorithms as interchangeable objects (composition). Template Method defines a skeleton algorithm in a base class with hook methods that subclasses override (inheritance).

questions.question: What is type erasure in Java generics and what are its implications?
options: Generics are erased at compile time
Generic type information is removed at runtime by the compiler — preventing runtime type checks on generic parameters
Generics are always preserved at runtime
Type erasure only affects primitive types
questions.correctAnswer: Generic type information is removed at runtime by the compiler — preventing runtime type checks on generic parameters
questions.explanation: Java compiles generics by replacing type parameters with their bounds (usually Object) and inserting casts. This means you cannot do instanceof on generic types or create generic arrays at runtime.
